The Station Strangler

By: Annalise Lubbe | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The Station Killer sodomised and strangled 22 boys 3 decades ago. Norman Simons, convicted on only one account, is now out on parole and living in Parow…parents fear for the safety of their children

Unique Selling Point:
In 1986, a faceless serial killer began stalking children on the Cape Flats. He became known as the Station Strangler. By 1994, 22 young boys had been found dead, sodomised and then strangled. The following year, in 1995, Norman Simons, a schoolteacher, was convicted of the murder of ten-year-old Elroy van Rooyen, the last victim in the string of child murders. In the public imagination, he was the Station Strangler. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, but the Supreme Court did not find in his favour. His conviction was upheld and his sentence was increased to life.

Summary:
After having spent 28 years in prison, Simons was released on parole on 20 July. He maintains his innocence, despite serving 28 years for the murder of Elroy van Rooyen. He is under house arrest living with a family member in an unknown location in Parow. He is allowed to leave the house to look for work or medical reasons provided he notifies his parole officer. This is no consolation for parents of young children who fear he might be up to his old tricks again. They are not convinced he is rehabilitated and may reoffend. South Africa has a 90% reoffending rate, one of the highest in the world. And with a half a dozen schools in close proximity in this neighbourhood and two railway lines running through the suburb, it is the perfect breeding ground for a criminal to commit the same crime again.
During a community meeting in Mitchells Plain and one in Parow prior to the release of Norman Simon from prison, Correctional Services and SAPS discussed the parole conditions and that he will be under house arrest. They also promised to re-open the cold cases of the 21 boys as there is now a special unit in SAPS who will be looking in more depth at the evidence which might lead them to the killers of the other 21 boys.


Further information:
Simons, described as a well dressed, soft spoken man who spoke several languages, suffered from depression and a staff member of Kenilworth Clinic, which he had been admitted to, reported him to the police. She believed he bore a likeness to an identikit compiled by a woman (Fiza Hendriks - who died) who had seen the two boys with the man while she waited for her daughter to return from the shop. Another lead came from Elroy’s cousin, Ryno who described the man they met at the station where Elroy disappeared when he boarded the train. When the identity kit appeared in the newspaper, Norman Jantjies, a resident of Mitchells Plain who took extra Xhosa classes from Norman Simons got to know the school teacher who only laughed when Jantjies pointed out the likelihood to Simons. Jantjies described Simons as a man who came across confident and was liked by his pupils.
Simons was never charged with any of the other killings. Nobody else was ever arrested. In 2010, police opened the cold case and re-investigated DNA samples taken from the crime scenes of the other 21 boys did not match that of Simons. However, this does not mean that he is innocent, according to Professor Gerard Labuschagne, the former head of the police's specialised Investigative Psychology Section. Instead, it could indicate that more than one person targeted little boys on the Cape Flats. Labuschagne and his team, which was the only unit mandated to profile offenders, reviewed the case material 13 years ago and could not find more evidence to link Norman Simons to the murder of the string of boys.
The Station Strangler was one of the most wanted men in the province in the early 1990s. Public pressure for an arrest was high and politicians vying for the coloured vote in the first democratic elections used the community's demand for justice as part of their political campaigning. As panic-stricken parents put pressure on authorities to make an arrest, an investigative team worked around the clock to find the child predator. After his arrest for Elroy's murder, Simons made a confession to police in which he claimed he had been sodomised as a child by his brother, who later died. Simons claimed his voice, however, instructed him to kill the children.
Norman Simon's admission: He claimed he could speak to the children “according to what I hear.” Victims would listen and carry out his instructions. “My personality then changes and I am capable of doing the wrong”. The killing started in 1986, and casualties were “innocent boys”. “”Many killings” followed in 1991, after the death of his brother. Murders were “brutal and the pain was awful”. During his trial, he did not testify in his own defense. This, according to Mike Stow, the prosecutor, was what sealed his fate. (The now retired prosecutor will not go on camera but talked me through the case).

Case studies:
Florence Gasant - Leroy’s Aunt: A broken family looking for answers why Elroy’s murderer is out on parole;
Louisa van Rooy - Grandmother of Elroy van Rooyen who looked after the boy
Shakir Smith - Chair: Parow West Neighbourhood Watch - about the safety of the community and parole conditions
Clifford Abel - Father of two boys is concerned about the safety of his family. They live in Parow West, a block away from a school.
Liza Etsebeth - Mother of a young boy and grade teacher at a nearby school, is fearful that there might be more victims now that Norman Simons lives in the neighbourhood where she always felt safe and her little boy was allowed to ride his bicycle in the streets. All this has changed now, she says.
Norman Jantjies: Chairman: Mitchell’s Plain United Residents Association (MURA) said the man has paid his dues……give him a chance to start a new life.
Prof Gerhard Labuschagne - Forensic and investigative psychologist: Expert opinion
Major General Bongani Maqashalala - Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation will address the question of reopening the cold cases of the 21 boys whose DNA did not match that of Norman Simons.

Script: The Station Strangler
Duration: 10 minutes

Up music and empty play parks

1 V/O Parow, north of Cape Town - a haven for families with children.
But after recent events, the atmosphere darkens here as a man dubbed the Station Strangler is released on parole.
PAUSE
He’s served two-thirds of a life sentence for sodomising and murdering a young boy…he’d confessed to killing others.

And this is his new home.

LINK: Norman Simons went from prison to Parow on parole a month ago. Some residents say he did his crime and served his time. But others fear for the safety of their children.

Clifford Abel: My first investigation was, where is he going to be? That was, for me, a concern.

Shakir Smith: People up in arms, people were afraid, we want to know this. We want to know that.

Liza Etsebeth: Knowing you live in the street or in the community with someone that hurts little children and especially boys, it's very concerning.

2 V/O For grade one teacher Liza Etsebeth, the fear is real.

Liza Etsebeth: Parent - I have to stress and I have to worry about where is this person staying? Where is my children going to get into contact with them? So it's alarming.

Erin Bates: Have there been talks in social circles or even in your professional circles around Simon's release into Parow?

Liza Etsebeth: Yes. Parents are very worried. We do not know what this person looks like and they can't share any information or pictures about him.

3 V/O Clifford Abel is a single parent.

Erin Bates: Your two sons, does this weigh on your mind when you think of Norman Simons being in Parow?

Clifford Abel: Yah, my sons is my priority in my life. So that is a great concern for me as a parent. Not knowing how his face look at this time and the government says he gets four hours outdoors to look for work or whatever it takes ten minutes to kidnap a child.

Fade to black

4 V/O The Station Strangler’s reign of terror swept the Cape Flats and surrounds in the late 80s and early 90s.
PAUSE
The bodies of 22 young boys discovered in shallow graves.

LINK: This is the station strangler secret graveyard. The bodies of more than a dozen victims were found here lying face down, hands tied behind their backs in shallow graves, sodomised and strangled.

Norman Jantjies: Chairman: Mitchells Plain Community Policing Forum - Not knowing when the next murder is going to take place, not knowing who's going to be the next victim and knowing that local children disappeared and they were murdered and raped.

5 V/O Norman Jantjies, at the time a young activist, joined in the search for missing boys - he’d attended Simons’ adult isiXhosa classes.

Norman Jantjies: He was very popular amongst his learners as such. He was regarded as a very good teacher, likable guy.

LINK: Norman Simons was a teacher here at Alpine Primary School here in Beacon Valley on the Cape Flats. He was said to be a quiet, unassuming and seemingly upstanding member of this community.

6 V/O It’s said he knew how to engage and befriend children, who surrounded him at school.
PAUSE CHANGE SCENE
It was in the coastal town of Strand, not far from the Cape Flats, that he encountered his young victim called Elroy van Rooyen.
The ten-year old lived with his grandmother. His aunt Florence Galant, who’d read about the so-called Station Strangler in the news, warned children to be weary of strangers.

Up sound

Florence Galant: Elroy’ aunt - En ek het hulle net gaan waarsku dat hulle moet versigtig wees wat hulle loop hulle klim in enige mens se kar want daar is a man wat kinders vang en kinders doodmaak. Spesifiek het Elroy gese, “maar Titi, daai man gaan nie vir my in die hande kry nie”.

SUBS: I just warned them to be careful
because when they walk
they can’t get into anyone’s car…
because there’s a man who’s
catching children and killing them.
Elroy’s words were “but Titi, that man won’t get me.”

7 V/O On a fateful afternoon, Elroy and his cousin Ryno were pushing trolleys for pocket money at a local mall. They were approached by a stranger who asked them to carry boxes to a nearby station for a tip.

Remembering the warnings, Ryno turned around. But Elroy didn’t. He boarded the train with the man and vanished. Granny Louise was beside herself.

Louisa van Rooy: Elroy’s granny: Ek se Ryno waar is Elroy, wat het van hom geword. Toe sou Ryno uitkom met die sak patats. En toe besluit ek, ek gaan nie saam met die man met die trein nie. Ek het gedink hy is seker maar op die stasie.

SUBS: I said “Ryno, where is Elroy?
What happened to him?”
That’s when Ryno spilled the beans:
“I decided not to go with the man on the train.
I thought he must be at the station.”

8 V/O Ten days later Elroy’s decomposing body was found in a veld close to a station. In the pocket of his blue tracksuit pants, his favourite toy: a spinning top.

LINK: The Station strangler lured victims from train stations and game arcades to their death. A handwritten note found in the trouser pocket’s of one of the boys read “one more, more to come”.

9 V/O There was no evidence on Elroy’s body linking him to his killer. Someone who’d seen a man with two boys on the day of Elroy’s disappearance helped the police compile an identikit. It later appeared in the papers.
PAUSE
It matched the appearance of the teacher, Norman Simons - who was arrested on charges of murder and sodomy.

Erin Bates: What was your reaction when you found out that he'd been charged?

Norman Jantjies: I was obviously shocked, but I also understood and it made perfect sense. He had the personality. He got along well with kids.

10 V/O Simons confessed to being sodomised by his late brother as a child. He said it had been his brother’s voice that instructed him to kill the children. Simons didn’t testify in his own trial and he was sentenced to life in prison.

Dr. Gérard Labuschagne: Most serial murderers will have a preferred victimology. Of course, if you are a paedophile and you want to rape and murder, you're going to be focusing on children.

11 V/O Forensic psychologist, DR. GÉRARD LABUSCHAGNE and his team reopened the case in 2010. But DNA technology wasn’t yet able to link Simons to the bodies of the other murdered children.

Erin Bates: What would be the differences between the kind of evidence available to investigators and the police in the 90s versus now?

DR. GÉRARD LABUSCHAGNE: Forensic investigative psychologist - Now we are able to obtain DNA from, you know, from a light touch on a door handle, fleeting contact. So the ability to get better DNA from smaller samples and less perfect samples is definitely improved with time.

12 V/O Pressure to re-open the case has mounted since Simons release and a task team has now been assembled. In the interim Deputy Provincial Commissioner for Crime Detection, Bongani Maqashalala , says the police aren’t letting down their guard.

Major General Bongani Maqashalala - Deputy provincial commissioner - Crime Detection Western Cape: Clip 005 - 14;02;00 Taking into account that the anger of the people when he was released. So it also became very important to government to ensure he is protected. 14;0216 He is under 24 hours arrest and he is monitored closely by a correctional service.

13 V/O It’s a necessary reassurance: In South Africa, a staggering 90% of those released from prison commit further crime. And sex offenders are high on the list.

Gerhard Labuschagne - 07;56;03 Sex offenders, child molesters are the highest re-offenders amongst most of the prison community. It's very difficult to change someone's sexual interest.

14 V/O Yet astonishingly the Justice Department told us the government's database of sex offenders is not available to the public.

Slight pause

That’s cause for concern in Parow.

Pause…Driving shot of Shakir neighbourhood watch

15 V/O While Simons is subject to strict parole conditions, he’s allowed eight contact visits a month. By agreement, Shakir Smith from Parow’s neighbour watch has to be informed of Simons’ whereabouts.

Erin Bates: What about a provision for him to go out and look for work?

Shakir Smith: Chairman: Parow West Neighbourhood Watch - If he does go out to look for work, he will have a caregiver with him constantly. I don’t know how that would work if he would find gainful employment. But let's face it, the guy's done 28 years…so as far as the justice system is concerned, he has done his time.

14 V/O Back in the Strand, granny holds a special place in her heart for little Elroy.

Louisa van Rooy: As ek partykeer so aleen is dan kry ek n gedagte as hy nou nog hier gewees het sou hy seker al kinders gehad het soos die ander en getroud gewees het.
Hy is nou weg. Wat baat dit om te huil en dit want hy is nie meer by ons nie.

SUBS: Sometimes, when I’m alone at night,
I consider… if he was still here, he’d probably have children,
like the others, and be married.
He’s gone.
What does it help to cry and all that…
because he’s not with us anymore.

___________________________________________________________________________

Promo 1: 21 seconds
V/O In the early nineties, a teacher named Norman Simons was found guilty of sodomising and strangling a young boy. 21 more bodies were found in that period. Simons was only convicted on one account.
Florence Galant: Hy het hull van hulle lewe gerob. Dit is wat dit is.
SUBS: He robbed them of life. That’s what it is.

Promo 2: 21 seconds
V/O 22 young boys were sodomised and strangled. A Cape Flats teacher was linked to the murder of only one and served 28 years in prison. Now out on parole he’s living in Parow.
Lisa Etsebeth: parent - 10 aug - clip 37 - 06;21;50 knowing you live in the street or in the community with someone that hurts little children and especially boys, it's very concerning.

Promo 3: 21 seconds
V/O Norman Simons, dubbed the station strangler, moved from prison to Parow with strict parole conditions. But parents fear for the safety of their children.
Clifford Abel: He has four hours outdoors to look for work or whatever. It takes ten minutes to kidnap a child.

He was said to be a quiet, unassuming and seemingly upstanding member of this community. 6 V/O It’s said he knew how to engage and befriend children, who surrounded him at school. PAUSE CHANGE SCENE It was in the coastal town of Strand, not far from the Cape Flats, that he encountered his young victim called Elroy van Rooyen. The ten-year old lived with his grandmother. His aunt Florence Galant, who’d read about the so-called Station Strangler in the news, warned children to be weary of strangers. Up sound Florence Galant: Elroy’ aunt - En ek het hulle net gaan waarsku dat hulle moet versigtig wees wat hulle loop hulle klim in enige mens se kar want daar is a man wat kinders vang en kinders doodmaak. Spesifiek het Elroy gese, “maar Titi, daai man gaan nie vir my in die hande kry nie”. SUBS: I just warned them to be careful because when they walk they can’t get into anyone’s car… because there’s a man who’s catching children and killing them. Elroy’s words were “but Titi, that man won’t get me.” 7 V/O On a fateful afternoon, Elroy and his cousin Ryno were pushing trolleys for pocket money at a local mall. They were approached by a stranger who asked them to carry boxes to a nearby station for a tip. Remembering the warnings, Ryno turned around. But Elroy didn’t. He boarded the train with the man and vanished. Granny Louise was beside herself. Louisa van Rooy: Elroy’s granny: Ek se Ryno waar is Elroy, wat het van hom geword. Toe sou Ryno uitkom met die sak patats. En toe besluit ek, ek gaan nie saam met die man met die trein nie. Ek het gedink hy is seker maar op die stasie. SUBS: I said “Ryno, where is Elroy? What happened to him?” That’s when Ryno spilled the beans: “I decided not to go with the man on the train. I thought he must be at the station.” 8 V/O Ten days later Elroy’s decomposing body was found in a veld close to a station. In the pocket of his blue tracksuit pants, his favourite toy: a spinning top. LINK: The Station strangler lured victims from train stations and game arcades to their death. A handwritten note found in the trouser pocket’s of one of the boys read “one more, more to come”. 9 V/O There was no evidence on Elroy’s body linking him to his killer. Someone who’d seen a man with two boys on the day of Elroy’s disappearance helped the police compile an identikit. It later appeared in the papers. PAUSE It matched the appearance of the teacher, Norman Simons - who was arrested on charges of murder and sodomy. Erin Bates: What was your reaction when you found out that he'd been charged? Norman Jantjies: I was obviously shocked, but I also understood and it made perfect sense. He had the personality. He got along well with kids. 10 V/O Simons confessed to being sodomised by his late brother as a child. He said it had been his brother’s voice that instructed him to kill the children. Simons didn’t testify in his own trial and he was sentenced to life in prison. Dr. Gérard Labuschagne: Most serial murderers will have a preferred victimology. Of course, if you are a paedophile and you want to rape and murder, you're going to be focusing on children. 11 V/O Forensic psychologist, DR. GÉRARD LABUSCHAGNE and his team reopened the case in 2010. But DNA technology wasn’t yet able to link Simons to the bodies of the other murdered children. Erin Bates: What would be the differences between the kind of evidence available to investigators and the police in the 90s versus now? DR. GÉRARD LABUSCHAGNE: Forensic investigative psychologist - Now we are able to obtain DNA from, you know, from a light touch on a door handle, fleeting contact. So the ability to get better DNA from smaller samples and less perfect samples is definitely improved with time. 12 V/O Pressure to re-open the case has mounted since Simons release and a task team has now been assembled. In the interim Deputy Provincial Commissioner for Crime Detection, Bongani Maqashalala , says the police aren’t letting down their guard. Major General Bongani Maqashalala - Deputy provincial commissioner - Crime Detection Western Cape: Clip 005 - 14;02;00 Taking into account that the anger of the people when he was released. So it also became very important to government to ensure he is protected. 14;0216 He is under 24 hours arrest and he is monitored closely by a correctional service. 13 V/O It’s a necessary reassurance: In South Africa, a staggering 90% of those released from prison commit further crime. And sex offenders are high on the list. Gerhard Labuschagne - 07;56;03 Sex offenders, child molesters are the highest re-offenders amongst most of the prison community. It's very difficult to change someone's sexual interest. 14 V/O Yet astonishingly the Justice Department told us the government's database of sex offenders is not available to the public. Slight pause That’s cause for concern in Parow. Pause…Driving shot of Shakir neighbourhood watch 15 V/O While Simons is subject to strict parole conditions, he’s allowed eight contact visits a month. By agreement, Shakir Smith from Parow’s neighbour watch has to be informed of Simons’ whereabouts. Erin Bates: What about a provision for him to go out and look for work? Shakir Smith: Chairman: Parow West Neighbourhood Watch - If he does go out to look for work, he will have a caregiver with him constantly. I don’t know how that would work if he would find gainful employment. But let's face it, the guy's done 28 years…so as far as the justice system is concerned, he has done his time. 14 V/O Back in the Strand, granny holds a special place in her heart for little Elroy. Louisa van Rooy: As ek partykeer so aleen is dan kry ek n gedagte as hy nou nog hier gewees het sou hy seker al kinders gehad het soos die ander en getroud gewees het. Hy is nou weg. Wat baat dit om te huil en dit want hy is nie meer by ons nie. SUBS: Sometimes, when I’m alone at night, I consider… if he was still here, he’d probably have children, like the others, and be married. He’s gone. What does it help to cry and all that… because he’s not with us anymore. ___________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1: 21 seconds V/O In the early nineties, a teacher named Norman Simons was found guilty of sodomising and strangling a young boy. 21 more bodies were found in that period. Simons was only convicted on one account. Florence Galant: Hy het hull van hulle lewe gerob. Dit is wat dit is. SUBS: He robbed them of life. That’s what it is. Promo 2: 21 seconds V/O 22 young boys were sodomised and strangled. A Cape Flats teacher was linked to the murder of only one and served 28 years in prison. Now out on parole he’s living in Parow. Lisa Etsebeth: parent - 10 aug - clip 37 - 06;21;50 knowing you live in the street or in the community with someone that hurts little children and especially boys, it's very concerning. Promo 3: 21 seconds V/O Norman Simons, dubbed the station strangler, moved from prison to Parow with strict parole conditions. But parents fear for the safety of their children. Clifford Abel: He has four hours outdoors to look for work or whatever. It takes ten minutes to kidnap a child. ________________________________________________________________________

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The Station Killer sodomised and strangled 22 boys 3 decades ago. Norman Simons, convicted on only one account, is now out on parole and living in Parow…parents fear for the safety of their children
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In 1986, a faceless serial killer began stalking children on the Cape Flats. He became known as the Station Strangler. By 1994, 22 young boys had been found dead, sodomised and then strangled. The following year, in 1995, Norman Simons, a schoolteacher, was convicted of the murder of ten-year-old Elroy van Rooyen, the last victim in the string of child murders. In the public imagination, he was the Station Strangler. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed, but the Supreme Court did not find in his favour. His conviction was upheld and his sentence was increased to life.
metadata.Summary: After having spent 28 years in prison, Simons was released on parole on 20 July. He maintains his innocence, despite serving 28 years for the murder of Elroy van Rooyen. He is under house arrest living with a family member in an unknown location in Parow. He is allowed to leave the house to look for work or medical reasons provided he notifies his parole officer. This is no consolation for parents of young children who fear he might be up to his old tricks again. They are not convinced he is rehabilitated and may reoffend. South Africa has a 90% reoffending rate, one of the highest in the world. And with a half a dozen schools in close proximity in this neighbourhood and two railway lines running through the suburb, it is the perfect breeding ground for a criminal to commit the same crime again. During a community meeting in Mitchells Plain and one in Parow prior to the release of Norman Simon from prison, Correctional Services and SAPS discussed the parole conditions and that he will be under house arrest. They also promised to re-open the cold cases of the 21 boys as there is now a special unit in SAPS who will be looking in more depth at the evidence which might lead them to the killers of the other 21 boys.
metadata.Further information: Simons, described as a well dressed, soft spoken man who spoke several languages, suffered from depression and a staff member of Kenilworth Clinic, which he had been admitted to, reported him to the police. She believed he bore a likeness to an identikit compiled by a woman (Fiza Hendriks - who died) who had seen the two boys with the man while she waited for her daughter to return from the shop. Another lead came from Elroy’s cousin, Ryno who described the man they met at the station where Elroy disappeared when he boarded the train. When the identity kit appeared in the newspaper, Norman Jantjies, a resident of Mitchells Plain who took extra Xhosa classes from Norman Simons got to know the school teacher who only laughed when Jantjies pointed out the likelihood to Simons. Jantjies described Simons as a man who came across confident and was liked by his pupils. Simons was never charged with any of the other killings. Nobody else was ever arrested. In 2010, police opened the cold case and re-investigated DNA samples taken from the crime scenes of the other 21 boys did not match that of Simons. However, this does not mean that he is innocent, according to Professor Gerard Labuschagne, the former head of the police's specialised Investigative Psychology Section. Instead, it could indicate that more than one person targeted little boys on the Cape Flats. Labuschagne and his team, which was the only unit mandated to profile offenders, reviewed the case material 13 years ago and could not find more evidence to link Norman Simons to the murder of the string of boys. The Station Strangler was one of the most wanted men in the province in the early 1990s. Public pressure for an arrest was high and politicians vying for the coloured vote in the first democratic elections used the community's demand for justice as part of their political campaigning. As panic-stricken parents put pressure on authorities to make an arrest, an investigative team worked around the clock to find the child predator. After his arrest for Elroy's murder, Simons made a confession to police in which he claimed he had been sodomised as a child by his brother, who later died. Simons claimed his voice, however, instructed him to kill the children. Norman Simon's admission: He claimed he could speak to the children “according to what I hear.” Victims would listen and carry out his instructions. “My personality then changes and I am capable of doing the wrong”. The killing started in 1986, and casualties were “innocent boys”. “”Many killings” followed in 1991, after the death of his brother. Murders were “brutal and the pain was awful”. During his trial, he did not testify in his own defense. This, according to Mike Stow, the prosecutor, was what sealed his fate. (The now retired prosecutor will not go on camera but talked me through the case). Case studies: Florence Gasant - Leroy’s Aunt: A broken family looking for answers why Elroy’s murderer is out on parole; Louisa van Rooy - Grandmother of Elroy van Rooyen who looked after the boy Shakir Smith - Chair: Parow West Neighbourhood Watch - about the safety of the community and parole conditions Clifford Abel - Father of two boys is concerned about the safety of his family. They live in Parow West, a block away from a school. Liza Etsebeth - Mother of a young boy and grade teacher at a nearby school, is fearful that there might be more victims now that Norman Simons lives in the neighbourhood where she always felt safe and her little boy was allowed to ride his bicycle in the streets. All this has changed now, she says. Norman Jantjies: Chairman: Mitchell’s Plain United Residents Association (MURA) said the man has paid his dues……give him a chance to start a new life. Prof Gerhard Labuschagne - Forensic and investigative psychologist: Expert opinion Major General Bongani Maqashalala - Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation will address the question of reopening the cold cases of the 21 boys whose DNA did not match that of Norman Simons. _________________________________________________________________________
